tree.title: Biology EOC Review
tree.description: Concept review for the NC Biology End-of-Course exam, organized by standard.

children.title: Heredity & Genetics
children.description: How meiosis and fertilization mix genes, how Punnett squares predict offspring, and how many genes plus the environment shape complex traits.

children.title: Meiosis & Genetic Variation
children.description: The two shuffles in meiosis that make every gamete unique.

teach.headline: Meiosis Shuffles the Genetic Deck
teach.body:
Meiosis makes haploid gametes and is a major source of **genetic variation**. Two mechanisms do the shuffling: **crossing-over**, where homologous chromosomes swap matching segments, and **independent assortment**, where chromosome pairs line up in random orientations.

Both mean every gamete carries a unique mix of alleles — part of why no two siblings (other than identical twins) are quite alike.

![Diagram of chromosomal crossover during meiosis](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_crossing_over.svg)

figures.alt: Homologous chromosomes exchanging segments during crossing-over in meiosis
figures.caption: Crossing-over swaps alleles between homologous chromosomes, increasing variation.

teach.mnemonic: CROSSING-OVER = SWAP SEGMENTS. INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT = SHUFFLE PAIRS. Every gamete is a new hand.
teach.poweredIdea: Meiosis creates genetic variation through crossing-over and independent assortment of chromosomes.

data.prompt: When homologous chromosomes exchange matching segments during meiosis, the process is called _____.
In the diagram, homologous chromosomes exchange matching segments during _____.
data.hint: The process shown between paired chromosomes

data.story: During meiosis, homologous chromosomes swap segments through crossing-over.
data.question: How does crossing-over most affect the resulting offspring?
data.answer: It increases genetic variation among the offspring.
options: It increases genetic variation among the offspring.
It makes all offspring genetically identical.
It doubles the chromosome number of each gamete.
It removes all the recessive alleles.
data.explanation: Swapping segments creates new allele combinations, increasing variation among gametes and offspring.

data.correct: Random lineup of chromosome pairs during meiosis
distractors: Exact copying of a DNA strand

data.story: Two siblings have the same two parents but look quite different from each other.
data.question: Which best explains this genetic difference?
data.answer: Meiosis and fertilization produce unique combinations of alleles in each offspring.
options: Meiosis and fertilization produce unique combinations of alleles in each offspring.
Each sibling has completely different DNA from the parents.
Mitosis gave each sibling a random set of genes.
The siblings' DNA mutated identically at birth.
data.explanation: Crossing-over, independent assortment, and the random pairing of gametes give each child a unique mix.

achievement.flavor: You name the two shuffles in meiosis that make every gamete — and every sibling — a new combination.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.6.1 (meiosis and sources of genetic variation). Maps to released item #20 (crossing-over increases variation). Deeper than the bundled scan content; no biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Gametes & Fertilization
children.description: How two half-sets combine into a full set with genes from both parents.

teach.headline: Two Halves Make a Full Set
teach.body:
Gametes (egg and sperm) are **haploid (n)** — they carry one set of chromosomes. **Fertilization** combines a haploid egg and a haploid sperm into a **diploid (2n)** zygote, restoring the full chromosome number.

That is why you inherit half your DNA from each parent: the zygote you started as was one gamete from each, joined together.
teach.mnemonic: n + n = 2n. HAPLOID EGG + HAPLOID SPERM → DIPLOID ZYGOTE. Half from each parent.
teach.poweredIdea: Fertilization joins two haploid gametes into a diploid zygote, mixing both parents' genes.

data.prompt: The joining of a haploid egg and a haploid sperm to form a diploid zygote is called _____.

data.story: A human egg carries 23 chromosomes and a human sperm carries 23 chromosomes. They fuse during fertilization.
data.question: How many chromosomes will the resulting zygote have?
options: 46 (diploid)
23 (haploid)
data.explanation: Fertilization adds the two haploid sets: 23 + 23 = 46, the diploid number for humans.

distractors: Identical to a normal body cell

data.story: One process produces gametes with half the chromosome number; another restores the full number in the next generation.
data.question: Which pairing is correct?
data.answer: Meiosis makes the haploid gametes; fertilization restores the diploid number.
options: Meiosis makes the haploid gametes; fertilization restores the diploid number.
Mitosis makes the gametes; meiosis restores the diploid number.
Fertilization makes the gametes; mitosis halves the number.
Meiosis both makes gametes and doubles the chromosome number.
data.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make gametes; fertilization recombines two gametes back to diploid.

achievement.flavor: You add two haploid sets into one diploid zygote and see why half your DNA came from each parent.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.6.1. Maps to released items #36 (fertilization restores diploid) and #19 (meiosis vs the process restoring number). Reworded, not reproduced. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Alleles, Genotype & Phenotype
children.description: Dominant and recessive alleles, and the difference between genotype and phenotype.

teach.headline: Dominant Hides, Recessive Waits
teach.body:
An organism carries two **alleles** for each gene, one from each parent. A **dominant** allele shows whenever it is present; a **recessive** allele shows only when both alleles are recessive.

**Genotype** is the allele combination (like Tt); **phenotype** is the visible trait (like tall). **Homozygous** means two identical alleles; **heterozygous** means two different ones.

![Autosomal recessive pedigree chart](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_pedigree.svg)

figures.alt: Pedigree chart showing autosomal recessive inheritance across three generations
figures.caption: Two unaffected carrier parents can have an affected child when a trait is recessive.

teach.mnemonic: BIG LETTER BULLIES the little one (dominant masks recessive). GENOTYPE = letters, PHENOTYPE = look.
teach.poweredIdea: Genotype is the allele pair; phenotype is the visible trait; recessive shows only when homozygous.

data.prompt: An organism with two different alleles for a trait (for example, Tt) is _____ for that trait.
In the pedigree diagram, two unaffected parents with an affected child suggest a _____ trait.
data.hint: The affected child inherited two hidden alleles

canonical.poweredIdea: Two unaffected parents producing an affected child is the hallmark of a recessive trait.

hints: Are either of the parents affected?
Can two unaffected parents have an affected child?

data.story: Two tall pea plants are crossed, and some of their offspring are short.
data.question: What does this reveal about the short trait?
data.answer: Short is recessive, and both tall parents carried a hidden recessive allele.
options: Short is recessive, and both tall parents carried a hidden recessive allele.
Short is dominant over tall.
The short offspring must have a mutation neither parent carried.
Tall and short are controlled by completely different genes.
data.explanation: Two tall (dominant-looking) parents producing short offspring means each parent was heterozygous and short is recessive.

achievement.flavor: You read a pedigree and realize two unaffected parents can hide a recessive allele between them.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.6.2/7.1 (genotype-phenotype, dominant/recessive). Maps to released item #37 (two tall parents, short child reveals recessive). Pedigree-detective interactive. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Punnett Squares & Ratios
children.description: Predicting offspring genotypes and phenotype ratios from a cross.

teach.headline: Predicting Offspring Combinations
teach.body:
A **Punnett square** predicts the probability of offspring genotypes. Put each parent's possible gametes on the sides, fill the boxes, and count the ratios.

For **ABO blood type**, alleles Iᴬ and Iᴮ are **codominant** (both show) and i is recessive. So a cross between a type A parent (Iᴬi) and a type B parent (Iᴮi) can give type A, B, AB, or O children.

![Punnett square for ABO blood type cross](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_punnett_blood_types.svg)

figures.alt: Punnett square showing possible ABO blood types from an IA i cross with an IB i parent
figures.caption: Codominant IA and IB alleles produce four possible blood types in offspring.

teach.mnemonic: GAMETES ON THE SIDES, COMBINE IN THE BOXES. Count the boxes = the odds for each offspring.
teach.poweredIdea: A Punnett square uses each parent's gametes to predict offspring genotype and phenotype ratios.

data.scenario: Cross a type A parent (IA i) with a type B parent (IB i). What blood types are possible in their children?
data.notes: Each child has a 1 in 4 chance of type AB, A, B, or O. IA and IB are codominant; i is recessive.

data.prompt: In the Punnett square diagram, each box shows one possible offspring _____.
data.hint: The allele combination, not just the visible trait

data.prompt: A diagram used to predict the genotypes of offspring from a genetic cross is a _____ square.

data.story: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). A heterozygous tall plant (Tt) is crossed with a short plant (tt).
data.question: What ratio of tall to short offspring is expected?
options: About 1 tall : 1 short
All tall offspring
About 3 tall : 1 short
All short offspring
data.explanation: Tt × tt gives half Tt (tall) and half tt (short), a 1:1 ratio.

distractors: All offspring show the recessive trait

achievement.flavor: You line up gametes and read the odds, even for a codominant blood-type cross with four outcomes.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.7.1 (Mendelian inheritance, Punnett squares). Maps to released item #21 (ABO blood-type cross). Punnett-builder interactive; phenotypeMap covers both allele orderings. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Incomplete Dominance & Codominance
children.description: When heterozygotes look blended or show both alleles at once.

teach.headline: Not Every Cross Is Tall vs Short
teach.body:
**Incomplete dominance:** heterozygotes show a **blended** phenotype. Red cattle (RR) crossed with white (rr) produce **roan** offspring (Rr) — a mix of red and white hairs.

**Codominance:** both alleles are **fully expressed** at once. Type AB blood shows both A and B antigens — not a blend.

**Multiple alleles:** ABO blood has three common alleles (I^A, I^B, i). Compare roan (blend) with type AB (both visible).
teach.mnemonic: INCOMPLETE = BLEND (roan). CODOMINANT = BOTH SHOW (type AB). Neither is simple dominant/recessive.
teach.poweredIdea: Incomplete dominance blends phenotypes; codominance expresses both alleles fully.

data.scenario: Cross two roan cattle (Rr × Rr). What coat-color phenotypes appear in the offspring?
data.notes: Incomplete dominance: Rr is roan (blended), not red. Expect 1 red : 2 roan : 1 white.

data.story: A person with type AB blood has both A and B antigens on their red blood cells.
data.question: Which inheritance pattern does type AB blood illustrate?
data.answer: Codominance — both alleles are fully expressed.
options: Codominance — both alleles are fully expressed.
Incomplete dominance — a blended intermediate phenotype.
Sex-linked inheritance on the X chromosome.
Polygenic inheritance from many genes.
data.explanation: Type AB shows both A and B antigens at once; neither allele is hidden or blended.

data.term: Roan cattle coat (Rr shows a mix of red and white hairs)

data.paragraph: Codominance means a heterozygote shows a blended intermediate phenotype, like pink flowers from red and white parents.
data.bugPhrase: Codominance means a heterozygote shows a blended intermediate phenotype
data.hint: Does type AB blood look blended, or do both antigens show?
data.canonicalFix: A blended intermediate is incomplete dominance (e.g., roan cattle). Codominance means both alleles are fully expressed at once (e.g., type AB blood).
data.poweredIdea: Blended = incomplete dominance; both fully visible = codominance.

data.term: Type AB blood (both A and B antigens visible)

achievement.flavor: You separate a roan blend from type AB showing both alleles at once.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.7.2 (incomplete dominance, codominance). Roan cattle punnett-builder; AB blood codominance scenario. Module-only on 2025 form — no released item tests roan or codominance vs incomplete. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Sex-Linked Inheritance
children.description: Genes on the X chromosome — colorblindness and hemophilia patterns.

teach.headline: Genes on the X Chromosome
teach.body:
**Sex-linked** (X-linked) traits are carried on the **X chromosome**. Males (XY) have only one X, so a single recessive allele on that X is expressed. Females (XX) need two copies to show a recessive X-linked trait.

**Colorblindness** and **hemophilia** are classic X-linked recessive traits. Carrier females are often unaffected but can pass the allele to sons.

Key rule: an affected X-linked recessive male got his X from his **mother** — **fathers do not pass X-linked alleles to sons**.

![Pedigree diagram showing inheritance across generations](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_pedigree.svg)

figures.alt: Pedigree chart with squares for males, circles for females, and filled symbols for affected individuals
figures.caption: Pedigrees track how a trait passes through families across generations.

teach.mnemonic: MALES HAVE ONE X — ONE RECESSIVE ALLELE SHOWS. DAD'S X GOES TO DAUGHTERS, NOT SONS.
teach.poweredIdea: X-linked recessive traits appear more often in males; fathers do not pass them to sons.

canonical.poweredIdea: X-linked recessive: affected males, carrier females, no father-to-son transmission.

hints: Are more males than females affected?
Can an affected father pass this trait directly to his son?

data.story: A woman is a carrier for hemophilia (X^H X^h). She has children with an unaffected man (X^H Y).
data.question: What is the probability their son has hemophilia?
data.answer: 50% — sons inherit their X from the mother.
options: 50% — sons inherit their X from the mother.
0% — fathers pass hemophilia to sons.
100% — all children of a carrier are affected.
25% — the same as a standard Punnett square for autosomal traits.
data.explanation: Sons get X from mother and Y from father. A carrier mother gives X^h half the time, so half of sons are affected.

data.prompt: A gene located on the X chromosome is described as _____ inheritance.

data.term: X-linked recessive trait in a family
data.correct: Affected males more common; no father-to-son transmission
distractors: Affected females more common than males
Every affected child has an affected parent
Passed from fathers to all sons

data.story: A woman has normal color vision but her father is colorblind and her mother has normal color vision.
data.question: What is her most likely genetic status for colorblindness?
data.answer: She is a carrier — she inherited her father's X with the colorblind allele.
options: She is a carrier — she inherited her father's X with the colorblind allele.
She is affected — daughters always show X-linked recessive traits.
She cannot be a carrier because she has normal vision.
She inherited the trait from her mother on an autosome.
data.explanation: Daughters get one X from each parent. A colorblind father gives every daughter his affected X — making them carriers if the trait is recessive.

achievement.flavor: You read an X-linked pedigree and know an affected son's allele came through his mother.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.7.2 (sex-linked traits). Pedigree-detective for X-linked recessive colorblindness; hemophilia cross scenario. Module-only on 2025 form. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Pedigrees & Genetic Disorders
children.description: Reading pedigrees for autosomal dominant and recessive disorders.

teach.headline: Pedigrees Reveal Inheritance Patterns
teach.body:
A **pedigree** tracks a trait through generations. Squares = males, circles = females, filled symbols = affected.

**Autosomal dominant** (e.g., Huntington disease): every affected person has at least one affected parent; trait appears every generation.

**Autosomal recessive** (e.g., cystic fibrosis): trait can **skip generations** — two unaffected parents can have an affected child if both are carriers.

![Pedigree diagram showing inheritance across generations](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_pedigree.svg)

figures.alt: Pedigree chart with squares for males, circles for females, and filled symbols for affected individuals
figures.caption: Filled symbols mark affected individuals; open symbols are unaffected.

teach.mnemonic: DOMINANT = NO SKIP — affected child, affected parent. RECESSIVE = CAN SKIP — two carriers, affected child.
teach.poweredIdea: Pedigree shape reveals autosomal dominant (no skip) vs recessive (can skip generations).

canonical.poweredIdea: Autosomal dominant: every affected person has an affected parent; no skipping.

hints: Does every affected person have at least one affected parent?
Can two unaffected parents have an affected child in this pedigree?

canonical.poweredIdea: Autosomal recessive can skip a generation — two unaffected parents can have an affected child.

hints: Can two unaffected parents have an affected child?
Does the trait skip a generation anywhere?

data.story: Two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis.
data.question: What must be true about both parents?
data.answer: Both are carriers — each has one recessive allele.
options: Both are carriers — each has one recessive allele.
One parent must be affected for the child to be affected.
The child must have a new mutation unrelated to the parents.
At least one parent must be homozygous dominant.
data.explanation: Autosomal recessive traits require two recessive alleles. Unaffected carrier parents (Aa × Aa) can produce an affected child (aa).

data.term: Every affected person has an affected parent

data.prompt: In the pedigree diagram, a filled (shaded) symbol means the individual is _____ for the trait.

achievement.flavor: You tell dominant from recessive by whether the trait skips a generation.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.7.3 (pedigrees and genetic disorders). Huntington autosomal-dominant and CF autosomal-recessive pedigree-detective quizzes. Module-only on 2025 form. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Karyotypes & Nondisjunction
children.description: Reading chromosome spreads, trisomy, and sex chromosome identification.

teach.headline: A Snapshot of Every Chromosome
teach.body:
A **karyotype** arranges an organism's chromosomes by size and shape. It reveals **extra or missing chromosomes** caused by **nondisjunction** — chromosomes failing to separate during meiosis.

**Trisomy 21** (three copies of chromosome 21) causes **Down syndrome**. Count the chromosomes: a normal human karyotype has **46** (22 pairs + XX or XY).

**XX** = female; **XY** = male — read the sex chromosomes in the lower-right of the spread.

![Human karyotype showing trisomy 21](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_karyotype.svg)

figures.alt: Human karyotype with chromosomes arranged by size; chromosome 21 shows three copies indicating trisomy 21
figures.caption: Three copies of chromosome 21 indicate trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).

teach.mnemonic: KARYOTYPE = CHROMOSOME PHOTO ALBUM. Extra copy of 21 = Down. XX or XY tells sex.
teach.poweredIdea: Karyotypes reveal trisomy and sex chromosomes; nondisjunction in meiosis causes wrong chromosome numbers.

data.prompt: An extra copy of chromosome 21 on a karyotype indicates _____ syndrome.
In the karyotype diagram, three copies of chromosome 21 indicate trisomy _____.
data.hint: Which chromosome has the extra copy?

data.story: A karyotype shows 22 pairs of autosomes plus two X chromosomes and no Y chromosome.
data.question: What is this individual's biological sex?
options: Female (XX)
Male (XY)
Cannot be determined from a karyotype
Intersex — always has both X and Y
data.explanation: Two X chromosomes and no Y indicate a female karyotype.

data.paragraph: Nondisjunction during mitosis is the usual cause of trisomy 21, because body cells fail to split chromosome 21 pairs evenly.
data.bugPhrase: Nondisjunction during mitosis is the usual cause of trisomy 21
data.hint: Which division makes gametes with half the chromosome number?
data.canonicalFix: Trisomy 21 usually starts when nondisjunction during meiosis produces a gamete with an extra chromosome 21. Fertilization then creates a zygote with three copies.
data.poweredIdea: Nondisjunction in meiosis creates gametes with wrong chromosome counts, leading to trisomy at fertilization.

data.correct: Down syndrome — three copies of chromosome 21

achievement.flavor: You spot an extra chromosome 21 and name the nondisjunction that put it there.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.7.3 (genetic disorders/karyotype) and LS.Bio.6.1 (chromosome structure). Trisomy 21 diagram-backed quizzes; nondisjunction debug-the-claim. Module-only on 2025 form. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Polygenic & Complex Traits
children.description: Why many traits come in a smooth range instead of two clean categories.

teach.headline: Many Genes, a Range of Outcomes
teach.body:
Some traits are **polygenic** — controlled by many genes acting together. Human **height** and skin color are classic examples.

Polygenic traits show **continuous variation**: a smooth range of phenotypes rather than two clear categories. They usually form a bell-shaped curve, with most people near the middle and only a few at the extremes.

![Bell curve showing continuous variation in a polygenic trait](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_polygenic_curve.svg)

figures.alt: Normal distribution bell curve with most individuals near the mean and fewer at the extremes
figures.caption: Polygenic traits cluster in the middle; extreme phenotypes are rare.

teach.mnemonic: MANY GENES = MANY STEPS = a SMOOTH RANGE. Bell curve: crowd in the middle, rare at the ends.
teach.poweredIdea: Polygenic traits are controlled by many genes and form a continuous range, with rare extremes.

data.prompt: A trait controlled by many genes acting together is described as _____.
In the diagram, most individuals cluster near the middle of the bell curve because polygenic traits show _____ variation.
data.hint: A smooth range, not just two categories

data.story: Human height varies smoothly across a whole range, not just 'tall' or 'short' like a single Mendelian trait.
data.question: What best explains this smooth range of heights?
data.answer: Height is polygenic — many genes contribute, producing continuous variation.
options: Height is polygenic — many genes contribute, producing continuous variation.
Height is controlled by a single dominant allele.
Height is not inherited at all.
Only the environment determines height, not genes.
data.explanation: Many genes each adding a small effect produce a continuous spread instead of two categories.

data.paragraph: Human height is controlled by a single gene with one tall allele and one short allele, exactly like Mendel's pea plants.
data.bugPhrase: controlled by a single gene with one tall allele and one short allele
data.hint: Does height come in just two categories, or a whole range?
data.canonicalFix: Human height is polygenic — many genes contribute, and the environment matters too — which is why it forms a continuous range rather than two categories.
data.poweredIdea: Continuous traits like height come from many genes, not a single dominant/recessive pair.

data.story: In a large population, both very short and very tall people are uncommon, while most people are near average height.
data.question: Why are the extreme heights rare?
data.answer: Polygenic traits cluster around the middle, so the extreme combinations of many genes are rare.
options: Polygenic traits cluster around the middle, so the extreme combinations of many genes are rare.
Extreme heights are caused only by mutations.
Tall and short are recessive while average is dominant.
The environment cannot affect a polygenic trait.
data.explanation: With many genes, most people land near the average; lining up many 'tall' or many 'short' alleles at once is uncommon.

achievement.flavor: You explain a smooth range of heights as many genes adding up, not a single tall-or-short switch.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.7.2 (polygenic/complex traits). Maps to released items #38 (height polygenic) and #39 (rare extreme phenotypes). Debug-the-claim targets the 'single gene controls height' trap. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Genes & the Environment
children.description: Why the same genes can produce different traits in different conditions.

teach.headline: Your Genes Aren't the Whole Story
teach.body:
**Phenotype = genotype + environment.** Even with the same genes, conditions change how a trait turns out. Human height depends on genes *and* on nutrition during growth.

Genetically identical organisms (clones) raised in different environments can look different. A trait you see is really a conversation between DNA and the world it develops in — your height is part genes, part dinner plate.
teach.mnemonic: GENES PROPOSE, ENVIRONMENT DISPOSES. Same DNA + different conditions = different phenotype.
teach.poweredIdea: Phenotype comes from genotype and environment together — the same genes can give different results.

data.scenario: Two genetically identical plants (clones) are grown for a season — one in rich soil with full sun, the other in poor soil and deep shade.
data.predictPrompt: How will the two clones most likely compare at the end of the season?
predictOptions: They will look identical because their DNA is identical
They will differ in size and health because environment shapes phenotype
Their DNA will change to match their environments
Only the shaded plant will have different genes
data.runNarrative: The clone in rich soil and sun grows larger and healthier; the one in poor soil and shade grows smaller. Their genes are the same, but the environment shaped how those genes were expressed.
data.truthSummary: Identical genotypes can produce different phenotypes when the environment differs.

bugCandidates.label: I assumed identical DNA must produce an identical appearance
bugCandidates.explanation: Phenotype depends on genotype AND environment, so identical genes can still look different in different conditions.

bugCandidates.label: I thought the environment rewrites the plants' DNA
bugCandidates.explanation: The environment changes how genes are expressed; it does not change the DNA sequence here.

bugCandidates.label: I assumed only one plant would be a true clone
bugCandidates.explanation: Both are genuine clones with identical DNA; the difference is purely environmental.

data.poweredIdea: Clones with identical DNA can still differ in phenotype when raised in different environments.

data.prompt: An organism's observable traits come from its genotype together with its _____.

data.story: Two people inherited similar sets of height genes, but one grew up much taller than the other.
data.question: What most likely explains the difference?
data.answer: Environmental factors such as nutrition during growth affected their height.
options: Environmental factors such as nutrition during growth affected their height.
One of them has completely different DNA now.
Height is unaffected by anything but genes.
Their genes mutated to make them different heights.
data.explanation: Height is shaped by genes and environment; differences in nutrition can lead to different adult heights even with similar genes.

data.term: Identical twins raised apart with very different diets
data.correct: May differ in traits like height because of the environment
distractors: Must be identical in every single trait
Have different DNA from each other

achievement.flavor: You treat a visible trait as a conversation between DNA and the conditions it grows up in.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.7.3 (genotype x environment). Maps to released items #40 (environment/nutrition affects height) and #46 (clones differ by environment). Predict-run-reflect targets the 'identical genes = identical look' trap. No biochem.* id reuse.
